unit.title: Perform thermal straightening, curling and waving

summary: This unit teaches you to straighten, curl and wave hair with heat: consult and check the scalp and hair, prepare the hair, test and control the heat of pressing combs and irons, press and flat-iron safely, make thermal curls and waves, avoid and recognise heat damage, deal with burns, and give aftercare. It also covers electrical safety, cleaning thermal tools and caring for natural, relaxed and fine hair.

blocks.p: Thermal styling uses heat to change the shape of hair for a short time. A pressed head of hair, a silk press or a set of shiny curls is one of the most requested services in a Jamaican salon, especially for weddings, graduations, church and work. It is also one of the services where clients get burnt and where hair is damaged for good. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees.

Thermal styling is **temporary**. Unlike a relaxer, it does not change the strong bonds in the hair, so the hair goes back to its natural shape when it gets wet or damp. That is both its advantage (no permanent change) and its limit (it does not last). Good thermal work depends on **dry, clean, protected hair, controlled heat and gentle hands**.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon: a soft press with a pressing comb finished with thermal curls, and a silk press with a flat iron with curls and waves. The assessor watches your heat testing, scalp and ear protection, small sections, tool safety and clean-up as well as the finished hair.

blocks.p: Inside each hair, long keratin fibres are held in shape by bonds. Two kinds matter here.

head: Bond
Strength
What changes it
Result
rows: Hydrogen bonds
Weak, but very many.
Water and heat.
Temporary: they break when the hair is wet or heated, and re-form as it dries or cools in a new shape.
Salt bonds
Weak.
Acids, alkalis, water.
Temporary.
Disulphide bonds
Strong, fewer.
Chemicals only: relaxers, perms.
Permanent. Heat styling does not break them.

ul: When a hot comb, iron or curling iron passes through **dry** hair, the heat breaks many hydrogen bonds and the hair takes the shape of the tool. As the hair cools, the bonds re-form in the new shape.
The natural curl is held by the strong disulphide bonds, which heat does not change. So the curl is still there under the pressed shape.
When the hair gets wet, or takes in moisture from rain, sweat, steam or humid air, the hydrogen bonds break again and the hair goes back to its natural shape. This is called **reversion**.
That is why a press lasts only until the next shampoo or until the hair gets damp, and why it 'goes back' faster in Jamaica's hot, humid weather.
Extreme heat or heat used too often damages the keratin itself, and then the hair does not go back to its natural curl: this is **heat damage**.

head: Feature
Thermal straightening
Chemical relaxer
rows: Bonds changed
Hydrogen bonds
Disulphide bonds
Lasts
Until the hair gets wet or damp
Permanent; only new growth is natural
Risk
Burns, heat damage, reversion
Chemical burns, over-processing
Done in
This unit
A separate unit (chemical straightening)

head: Ask or check
Why
rows: The result she wants (soft press, silk press, curls, waves) and how long it must last
To choose the method and heat.
Chemical services, with dates: relaxer, colour, bleach, keratin treatments
Treated hair is weaker and needs less heat.
How often she uses heat at home and how hot; any past burns or damage
To judge the risk of heat damage.
Events: rain, sea, a wedding, a long day outdoors
Reversion risk; she may need a different plan.
The scalp: cuts, sores, burns, infection, tenderness
Heat on broken skin burns and hurts; infection must not be spread.
The hair: texture, density, porosity, elasticity, condition, breakage, split ends
Decides tool, heat setting and number of passes.
The edges and nape
Fine hair burns and breaks first.

head: Finding
What to do
rows: Cuts, sores, burns or an infection on the scalp
No thermal service today; refer if needed.
Signs of a contagious condition (lice, ringworm)
No service; refer kindly and privately.
Very weak, broken or heat-damaged hair
Postpone; give treatments; use the lowest heat only if the instructor agrees.
Hair that was recently relaxed, coloured or lightened, and is weak
Use lower heat; strand test.
Hair or scalp wet, or product build-up heavy
Do not use heat: dry and clean it first.

blocks.p: Flat irons and pressing combs vary by maker and by age, and the number on a dial may not be the real temperature. Use the guide below as a starting point, test on a tissue or towel, and follow the maker and your instructor.

head: Hair
Heat
Comment
rows: Fine, damaged, bleached, chemically treated or heat-damaged
Lowest setting
These burn and break easily. Keep passes few.
Medium texture, healthy, relaxed or coloured
Low to medium
Increase only if needed.
Coarse, thick, virgin natural hair
Medium to higher, but never as hot as the tool will go
Takes more heat, but heat damage still happens.
Edges, nape and baby hairs
Lower than the rest
The hair is finer and burns easily.

blocks.note: A common range for flat irons is roughly 150 to 200 degrees C for fine or treated hair and up to about 220 degrees C for coarse healthy hair; most damage starts above that. Always check the maker's guidance, and never use the highest setting 'to be safe'.

sections.title: Tools, heat testing and electrical safety

head: Tool
Description
Notes
rows: Pressing comb
A metal comb (brass, or steel) with a wooden or heat-proof handle; heated in a pressing comb heater or on a stove.
The **back (spine)** of the comb does most of the straightening; the teeth carry the hair. The wooden handle stays cool.
Comb heater (pressing stove)
Electric or gas unit that heats the comb.
Keep away from anything that can burn; do not leave it unattended.
Flat iron (straightening iron)
Two heated plates, ceramic, titanium or tourmaline, with a heat dial.
Check cord and plugs; plates clean; use the heat dial.
Curling iron (Marcel iron)
A rod and a shell (groove) that hold the hair; heated; used for curls and waves.
Keep a comb between the iron and the scalp.
Hot rollers
Rollers heated in a unit, used to set dry hair in curls.
Let them cool in the hair for the time the maker says.
Blow-dryer with comb nozzle
A dryer with a comb attachment to stretch the hair.
Stretches natural hair before a press.
Tail comb; wide-tooth comb; fine comb; clips
Parting and sectioning; detangling.
Hard rubber combs do not melt.
Heat mat / tool holder
A heat-resistant surface or stand.
Rest hot tools only here.

flow: Heat the comb or iron
Wipe it clean of residue
Touch it to a white tissue or towel for a second
If the tissue scorches or turns brown, it is too hot: let it cool and test again
If it only warms the tissue, it is ready

blocks.p: A white tissue or towel shows you at once whether the tool will scorch the hair. Test **every time** before the tool touches the hair, and again if the tool has been left on.

ul: Before use, check the **cord, plug and casing** for damage and that the plates are clean. Check the label to see that the tool suits the Centre's supply (Jamaica uses 110 V and 220 V, 50 Hz).
If a tool is damaged or sparks when you switch it on, **do not use it**: unplug it, label it faulty and report it.
Keep tools, plugs and extension cords **away from basins and water**. Dry your hands before touching plugs.
Keep cords **tidy and off the floor**, so nobody trips. Never wrap a cord round a hot tool.
Put hot tools down only in a **heat-resistant holder or on a heat mat**, never on towels, paper or the client.
Keep the comb heater away from flammable products and cloth. Never leave a hot tool alone.
Keep the area **ventilated**, to clear smoke and fumes from heated products.
At the end: switch off, **unplug**, and let tools cool in a safe place before cleaning and storing.

blocks.note: A flat iron left on, or a pressing comb left on a stove, is a fire hazard and a burn hazard for the next person. Make switching off and unplugging a habit before you take off your apron.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Preparing natural coily hair for a press

flow: Check the scalp is healthy
Shampoo gently to remove oil, dirt and build-up; product left on the hair burns and smokes
Apply a moisturising conditioner and detangle in sections from the ends up
Rinse; blot with a towel
Apply a heat protectant as the maker says
Blow-dry in sections with a comb nozzle, on a medium heat, to stretch the hair until it is completely dry
Divide into four main sections with a tail comb; clip
Work in small sub-sections

ul: **Clean:** oil, grease and build-up fry on hot hair, smell, smoke and weigh it down.
**Completely dry:** water on hair turns to steam under a hot iron and can burn the scalp and the hair (a steam burn, or scald). Hair that feels cool to your hand is not dry. Check the roots.
**Stretched:** blow-drying with a comb nozzle stretches the coils so that the press goes through smoothly with fewer passes and less heat.
**Protected:** a heat protectant helps shield the hair from heat damage. It does not make heat safe: you still need a suitable setting.

head: Product
Use
Rule
rows: Heat protectant
On clean, damp or dry hair before heat.
Use as the maker says.
Pressing oil or cream
A little on the sections to add shine and slip.
A **small amount** only: too much smokes, fries and weighs the hair down.
Thermal serum/shine spray
After the style.
Light, non-oily.
Setting lotion
For roller sets.
Not on hair about to be pressed.

head: Type
Passes
Use
rows: Soft press
One pass on each side of the section, light pressure.
Fine or fragile hair; a light, natural result.
Medium press
One pass on each side with a little more pressure.
Medium texture.
Hard (double) press
Two passes on each side, more heat and pressure.
Coarse, resistant hair. It adds extra heat, so it can damage and break the hair: do not do it often.

blocks.h: Pressing a section with a pressing comb

flow: Hair clean, completely dry, protected, sectioned
Heat the comb in the heater
Test on a white tissue or towel; if it scorches, let it cool and test again; wipe the comb clean
Take a small section; comb it smooth; add a very small amount of pressing oil if needed
Hold the section out from the head, away from the scalp
Put the teeth into the section near the root, without touching the scalp
Turn so that the back (spine) presses the hair; draw the comb slowly to the ends
Repeat on the other side for a soft or medium press as planned
Protect the ear by holding it down; use less heat at the edges

ul: Press **small sections** so the heat passes evenly through every hair.
Keep the comb moving. Never rest it on the hair.
Hold the section away from the scalp. The comb's heat and the steam from a damp spot can burn.
If you smell burning hair, **stop**, check the heat and lower it before you go on.

blocks.h: Silk press with a flat iron

flow: Shampoo, deep-condition, detangle, apply heat protectant
Blow-dry in sections with a comb nozzle until stretched and completely dry
Check the iron's cord and plug; make sure the plates are clean
Set the heat to suit the hair; test on a tissue or towel
Divide into four sections; take small sub-sections
Comb each sub-section smooth; use the **comb chase**: comb just ahead of the iron as it glides slowly from root to ends
Keep the plates away from the scalp and ears; make as few passes as you need
Rest the iron on a heat mat between sections
Check the hair is smooth from root to ends; finish the style
Switch off, unplug, cool and clean the iron

ul: A few smooth, steady passes are better than many quick ones: each pass adds heat to the same hair.
Do not clamp the iron and hold it still. Glide it.
A flat iron can also curl hair: turn it as it glides.

head: Type
How it is made
Result
rows: Croquignole curl
Hair wound from the ends up towards the scalp.
Curl is tighter at the ends; more volume at the bottom.
Spiral curl
Hair wound along the length of the iron, like a corkscrew.
Ringlets.
Marcel wave
S-shaped waves made with a hot Marcel iron, by alternate movements.
A smooth, shaped wave.
Flat iron curls and waves
A flat iron turned as it glides, or a pinch-and-twist.
Loose curls or waves.
Hot roller set
Heated rollers on dry hair; cool before removing.
Volume and curl.

blocks.h: Making a croquignole curl with a curling iron

flow: Hair clean, dry and protected; iron checked and tested on a tissue or towel
Take a small section, no wider than the iron; comb it smooth
Hold it out from the head at the angle for the volume you want
Open the iron, place it on the hair near the ends, and close it
Wind the hair from the ends up towards the scalp, turning the iron and moving the clamp slightly so the hair moves smoothly
Stop before the scalp; put a comb between the iron and the scalp
Hold the client's ear down and away
Hold for a few seconds, slide the iron out gently and let the curl cool, pinned if needed
When all the curls are cool, comb or brush them out

ul: **Why let a curl cool before combing it?** The hydrogen bonds re-form as the hair cools, setting the curl. If you comb it hot, the curl drops.
Never leave the iron on one section too long: hold only for the few seconds needed.
A comb between the iron and the scalp protects the scalp from burns.

blocks.h: Heat damage: signs, causes and prevention

head: Signs
Causes
Prevention
rows: Dry, rough, dull hair; split ends and breakage
Heat that is too high for the hair
Choose a heat to suit the hair; test on a tissue or towel.
Natural hair that no longer curls back after washing; straight or limp pieces
Many passes over the same section
Few smooth passes; small sections.
A smell of burning, a scorched look or colour change
Pressing damp hair; too much oil
Hair completely dry; a small amount of oil.
Bubbles or blisters along the hair shaft (bubble hair)
Heat on wet or damp hair
Check the roots are dry.
Hair snapping or thinning at the edges
Pressing too often; no protectant
Heat protectant; advise less frequent heat.

blocks.p: Heat-damaged hair does not grow back to its natural pattern: the damaged part must be cut off. Chemically treated, fine or damaged hair and the edges are most at risk. Prevent damage by checking the hair in the consultation, using protectant, testing the tool, and stopping at once if you smell burning.

flow: Stop the service; put the hot tool down safely and switch it off
Stay calm and reassure the client
Cool the burn under cool running water for about 20 minutes (or a clean cloth soaked in cool water if it is on the scalp and running water is hard to use)
Do not use ice, butter, oil, toothpaste or hair products; do not break blisters
Cover loosely with a clean, non-fluffy dressing if needed
Call the instructor or first aider; get medical help if the burn is large, deep, blistered or on the face
Write what happened in the accident book; find and fix the cause

blocks.note: A minor burn is cooled for about 20 minutes. Do not stop after a minute or two because it 'feels better'. If the burn is large, deep or on the face, or if the client is unwell, she must get medical help.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Smoke or burning smell from the hair
Stop; check the heat; lower it; test again.
A tool sparks
Unplug it, label it faulty, report it.
Hair breaks during pressing
Stop; check heat and moisture; tell the client.
Client says it is too hot
Move the tool away at once; check the heat and the distance from the scalp.

head: Advice
Why
rows: Keep the hair away from moisture, rain, steam and sweat
Water makes the hair revert.
Wrap it at night and cover with a satin or silk scarf or bonnet
Smooth fabric keeps it smooth; cotton drags and soaks up moisture.
Use light, non-water-based products, sparingly
Heavy products weigh the hair down; water-based ones can make it revert.
Do not press or flat iron again every few days; use protectant and low heat at home
Frequent high heat causes lasting damage.
Deep condition regularly and trim
Keeps the hair healthy.
Expect reversion in humid weather
It is normal, not a fault.

flow: Switch off, unplug and let the tools cool
Wipe the flat iron and curling iron plates with a damp cloth when cool, then disinfect as the maker says
Remove oil and carbon build-up from the pressing comb when it is cool, as the maker says
Wash and disinfect combs and clips
Store tools dry, with the cords loosely coiled, in a safe place

ul: Client, date, result wanted.
Scalp and hair findings: texture, density, porosity, elasticity, condition.
Heat setting used and why; type of press or curl; products used.
Any problem, burn or damage; advice given.
Client's agreement.
I can explain how heat changes hydrogen bonds, why the result is temporary and what reversion is.
I can say how thermal straightening differs from a relaxer.
I can consult, check the scalp and hair, and recognise contra-indications.
I can choose a heat setting to suit fine, treated, damaged, coarse and edge hair.
I can prepare natural hair: shampoo, condition, protect, blow-dry completely dry, and section.
I can heat and test a pressing comb or iron on a white tissue or towel and act on the result.
I can do a soft, medium and hard press and explain the difference.
I can give a silk press with a flat iron using the comb chase.
I can make croquignole and spiral curls and waves, with a comb between the iron and the scalp.
I can protect the scalp, ears and edges.
I can use electrical tools safely and report a faulty one.
I can recognise heat damage and prevent it.
I can give first aid for a burn and record it in the accident book.
I can give aftercare advice, clean and store thermal tools, and keep records.

blocks.note: In essay answers, link the step to the reason: 'The hair must be completely dry because water turns to steam under a hot iron and can burn the hair and the scalp.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Thermal styling
Changing the shape of hair with heat, for a short time.
Hydrogen bonds
Weak bonds in the hair that heat and water break and re-form.
Disulphide bonds
Strong bonds in the cortex that only chemicals change.
Reversion
Pressed hair going back to its natural curl when it gets wet or damp.
Heat protectant
A product that helps shield the hair from heat damage.
Pressing comb
A metal comb heated and drawn through the hair; the back straightens.
Soft, medium and hard press
One light pass, one firmer pass, or two passes on each side.
Silk press
A flat iron service on blow-dried natural hair for very smooth, shiny hair.
Comb chase
Combing just ahead of the flat iron as it glides.
Croquignole curl
A curl wound from the ends up towards the scalp.
Spiral curl
A curl wound along the length of the iron.
Marcel wave
An S-shaped wave made with a Marcel iron.
Heat mat
A heat-resistant surface for resting hot tools.
Scald
A burn from steam or hot liquid.
Heat damage
Lasting damage from too much heat, shown by dry, rough, broken hair that will not curl back.
Accident book
The record of accidents, such as burns, and what was done.

c1.title: A wedding press in Falmouth
c1.text: Camille Brown, 27, comes to a salon in Falmouth the day before a beach wedding. She wants her shoulder-length natural hair silk pressed. Her hair is fine at the edges and coarse at the back, healthy, and she uses a flat iron at home every other day on high. She says her hair 'never stays straight in the heat'. Trainee Tashane has shampooed and conditioned it and starts to blow-dry, but the roots at the nape still feel cool and slightly damp.

c2.title: A pressing comb in Old Harbour
c2.text: Trainee Joel is pressing the hair of Mrs. Elaine Foster, 60, whose hair is relaxed and thin. He has heated the pressing comb in the stove and tests it on a white tissue, which turns brown at once. Joel has no time and says the hair is thin so the heat will be quick. He holds the section close to the scalp. Mrs. Foster says the comb feels very hot near her ear.

c3.title: A burnt ear in Linstead
c3.text: During a practical session in the Centre's training salon, trainee Racquel is curling a model's hair with a curling iron when the iron touches the model's ear. The model cries out. There is a red mark on the top of her ear. The iron is lying on the model's towel on the shoulder cape.

c4.title: A scorched section in May Pen
c4.text: Dennis Reid, 33, in May Pen, has had his natural hair pressed every week for a year to look tidy for work. The hair at the front is dry and rough, and in places a few patches have stayed straight and limp after washing instead of curling back. Trainee Alecia plans to press it again today at the highest heat on the comb, using plenty of oil.

c5.title: Electrical safety in Spanish Town
c5.text: In the training salon in Spanish Town, a trainee plugs a flat iron into an extension cord that runs across a damp floor near the basin. The flat iron's cord is split, with wires showing at the plug end. It sparks when switched on. A pressing comb heater is next to a spray can of hairspray on the same trolley.

questions.q: What should Tashane do about the damp roots at the nape before she presses?
o: Press them quickly, as the heat of the comb will dry them
Add extra oil to the damp roots to protect against the heat
Keep drying until the roots are completely dry too
Press the dry parts first and come back to the nape later
questions.why: Water on hair turns to steam under a hot iron or comb and can scald the scalp and damage the hair. The roots must be checked and the hair completely dry before any heat touches it.

questions.q: What does Camille's habit of flat ironing every other day on high suggest?
o: A risk of heat damage, so use less heat and fewer passes
Her hair is now immune to heat, so higher settings are safe
She needs the highest heat to straighten her coarse hair
The salon should add extra oil to cover up any damage
questions.why: Frequent high heat is a main cause of heat damage. Asking about home heat use in the consultation shows the risk, and the salon then uses a suitable heat and advises her to cut down.

questions.q: Which setting is the best starting point for Camille's hair, if the maker gives no other guidance?
o: The highest setting for every section, because of the coarse back
One medium setting for every section, to keep things simple
The lowest setting, with six or more passes on every section
Less heat at the edges, more at the coarse back if needed
questions.why: Different parts of the head need different heat: fine edges burn and break first, coarse parts take more. Test the tool on a tissue and keep passes few; many passes add as much damage as high heat.

questions.q: Camille asks how long the press will last at the beach wedding. What is the most honest answer?
o: For ever, because a silk press changes the hair for good
Only until the hair gets damp; humidity can make it revert
About a month, whatever the weather or the activity
As long as a relaxer, because both use heat on the hair
questions.why: A thermal press changes only the weak hydrogen bonds, so moisture from humid air, sweat or water makes the hair revert. She should be told this and advised how to protect it.

questions.q: What does the brown tissue tell Joel?
o: The comb is at just the right heat for thin hair
The comb is too hot; let it cool and test it again
The comb is dirty and should be wiped, then used
The comb is cool and needs more time in the stove
questions.why: A scorching or browning tissue means the tool would scorch the hair. Let it cool and test again; testing is done before every use.

questions.q: Why is Joel's plan to press thin, relaxed hair at a high heat a poor choice?
o: Thin hair needs more heat because there is less of it
Relaxed hair cannot conduct heat, so it needs a hotter comb
Thin hair cannot be pressed at any heat, relaxed or not
Thin relaxed hair is weak and needs a lower heat setting
questions.why: Fine, relaxed or chemically treated hair is weaker and takes the lowest heat. 'Quick' heat on weak hair breaks it.

questions.q: What is wrong with how Joel is holding the section?
o: He should hold it out from the head, with the comb off the scalp
Nothing is wrong; holding it close to the scalp gives the straightest press
He should keep it close to the scalp but move the comb faster
He should rest the comb lightly on the scalp to judge the heat
questions.why: Holding the section out from the head and keeping the comb off the scalp prevents scalp burns, and the ear should be held down and protected.

questions.q: Mrs. Foster says the comb feels very hot near her ear. What should Joel do?
o: Tell her the heat will pass in a moment and carry on
Press faster round the ear so it is over quickly
Move the comb away at once, then check the heat
Carry on, but use a little less oil near the ear
questions.why: A client's report of heat is a warning. Stop, move the tool away, check and lower the heat, and shield the ear by holding it down.

questions.q: What should Racquel do first?
o: Hold ice against the burn straight away to stop it blistering
Rub butter on the ear to soothe it, then cover it up
Carry on with the curls on the other side, as the mark is small
Put the iron safely in a holder, switch off, then cool the burn
questions.why: Make the situation safe first, then cool the burn with cool running water. Ice, butter and oil are not used on burns.

questions.q: For how long should a minor burn like this be cooled?
o: About 20 seconds
About 20 minutes
Until the redness has gone completely
About 2 minutes
questions.why: A minor burn is cooled under cool running water for about 20 minutes. Stopping too soon allows the burn to deepen.

questions.q: Where should Racquel have put the hot iron when she was not using it?
o: On a folded towel next to the basin
On the shoulder cape, clear of the client's skin
On a heat mat or in a heat-resistant holder
On the trolley top, beside the other tools
questions.why: Hot tools rest only on a heat mat or in a heat-resistant holder. A towel can scorch or catch fire, and a tool left on a cape or loose on the trolley can fall or burn the client.

questions.q: After first aid, what else must Racquel do?
o: Write it in the accident book and tell the instructor at once
Nothing more is needed, since the burn was only a minor one
Tell the other trainees about it at the end of the day
Ask the model to sign that she moved her head and caused it
questions.why: Every accident is reported to the instructor and written in the accident book, so the cause can be found and fixed and there is a record.

questions.q: What do the patches that stay straight and limp after washing tell Alecia?
o: The hair is heat damaged and will not curl back there
The hair is healthy and just needs a deep treatment
The hair needs a stronger press to hold it straight
The hair is only dry and will recover within a week
questions.why: Hair that no longer curls back after washing has lost its natural pattern from too much heat. The damaged parts need to be trimmed and the hair rested.

questions.q: What should Alecia do instead of her plan?
o: Press again at a lower heat, but with plenty of oil
Use a hard press to get the damaged parts straight
Postpone it; advise a rest from heat, plus treatments
Use a much hotter iron, so that fewer passes are needed
questions.why: Damaged hair needs rest, treatments and trimming, not more heat. Advise him honestly and offer a protective or low-heat style.

questions.q: Why is plenty of oil on the hair a problem under a hot comb?
o: Oil cools the comb, so the press does not work
Too much oil smokes and fries onto the hair strands
Oil makes the hair curl up again as it dries
Oil is no problem at all as long as the comb is clean
questions.why: A small amount adds slip and shine. Too much cooks on the hair, smokes and leaves it greasy and heavy.

questions.q: Which aftercare advice would help Dennis the most?
o: Press every three days so that the hair always looks tidy
Wash with very hot water each day to remove the damage
Sleep with the hair wet so that it stays soft overnight
Use protectant and low heat, and press much less often
questions.why: Heat damage is prevented by less frequent heat, a protectant and low settings. Moisture treatments and a satin bonnet at night protect the hair.

questions.q: What should the trainee do with the flat iron with the split cord that sparks?
o: Use it quickly and carefully, keeping away from the wires
Not use it: unplug it, label it faulty and report it
Wrap tape round the split cord and use it for the press
Use it only on completely dry hair, away from the basin
questions.why: A damaged cord or a spark is an electric shock and fire risk. The tool is taken out of use, labelled and reported.

questions.q: What is wrong with the extension cord?
o: It lies across a damp floor near the basin: a shock risk
It is too short and will pull the iron off the trolley
It is a thin cord, so it should be doubled over to be safe
It is plugged into the wall, which overloads the socket
questions.why: Cords must be tidy, off the floor and away from water. A cable across a wet floor near a basin risks tripping and electric shock.

questions.q: What is the hazard in the pressing comb heater being next to a spray can?
o: None, as the heater is switched off at the time
The heater will cool the spray can down and spoil the spray
The spray will clean the comb as it heats in the heater
Aerosols are flammable and can burst when kept near heat
questions.why: Hairspray is flammable and a can can burst near heat. Keep heaters away from aerosols and anything that can burn.

questions.q: A client wants her hot-roller curls to last through an evening out. When should the rollers come out?
o: The moment the heater light goes off, while they are hot
After a quick spray of water, to cool them faster
After they have cooled in the hair as the maker says
Straight away, then pin the curls up wet
questions.why: Curls set as the hair cools and the hydrogen bonds re-form in the new shape. Taking rollers out hot, or wetting the hair, lets the curl drop.
